title: Conditional types
subtitle: T extends U ? X : Y, distribution, infer

cards.front: How do you read T extends U ? X : Y?
cards.meaning: At the type level, extends means is assignable to, not class inheritance. The conditional picks X if T is assignable to U, otherwise Y.
cards.example: type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

cards.front: What are IsString<'hello'> and IsString<42>?
cards.meaning: true and false. 'hello' is assignable to string; 42 is not. That is the basic type-level branch.
cards.example:
type A = IsString<'hello'>; // true
type B = IsString<42>; // false

cards.front: What do conditionals add that generics alone do not?
cards.meaning: Generics parameterize; conditionals branch on relationships between types. That lets you filter unions, unwrap wrappers, and pick APIs based on input shape.

cards.front: Which built-ins are powered by conditional types?
cards.meaning: Exclude, Extract, NonNullable, ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited, plus custom unwrap / branch-on-shape helpers. Utility types are consumers of this machinery.

cards.front: What does T extends { id: infer Id } ? Id : never capture?
cards.meaning: If T has an id property, infer binds Id to that property's type and the true branch returns it; otherwise never. Pattern for 'property type if present'.
cards.example: type IdOf<T> = T extends { id: infer Id } ? Id : never;

cards.front: What is ToArray<string | number> when ToArray is T extends any ? T[] : never?
cards.meaning: When T is a naked type parameter and a union, the conditional distributes once per member: string[] | number[], not (string | number)[]. Evaluation is ToArray<string> | ToArray<number>. This is how Exclude and Extract filter unions.
cards.example: type Result = ToArray<string | number>; // string[] | number[]

cards.front: When does a conditional distribute over a union?
cards.meaning: Only when the checked type is a naked type parameter — just T, not wrapped in a tuple, array, or similar — and T is a union. Distribution runs the conditional once per member, then unions the results. Distribution is only for naked type params in the checked position.

cards.front: How do you treat a union as one unit in a conditional?
cards.meaning: Wrap the type parameter so it is not naked, e.g. [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never. Then ToArrayNonDist<string | number> is (string | number)[], not string[] | number[].

cards.front: How is Exclude implemented?
cards.meaning: MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T. Each union member is tested; matches become never and disappear from the union. That is the filter trick behind Exclude. Do not reinvent it for ordinary union filtering.

cards.front: How is Extract implemented?
cards.meaning: MyExtract<T, U> = T extends U ? T : never. Members assignable to U are kept; the rest become never and vanish. Complementary to Exclude.

cards.front: Why does never disappear from union results?
cards.meaning: never members vanish from unions. Rejected conditional branches use never so filtered members disappear — the mechanism Exclude and Extract rely on.

cards.front: What does infer do?
cards.meaning: Inside an extends clause, infer Name introduces a new type variable bound to whatever matched that position, usable in the true branch. You cannot use infer outside an extends clause.
cards.notes: Using infer outside extends is a listed misconception.

cards.front: What is ElementType<string[]> vs ElementType<string>?
cards.meaning: string, and never. ElementType<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never infers the array element when T matches an array; otherwise the false branch is never.
cards.example:
type A = ElementType<string[]>; // string
type C = ElementType<string>; // never

cards.front: How do you flatten one level of an array type without turning non-arrays into never?
cards.meaning: T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T — unwrap the element if T is an array, otherwise keep T. That differs from ElementType, which uses never on the false branch.

cards.front: How do you sketch ReturnType with infer?
cards.meaning: F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never captures the return type R when F is a function type; otherwise never. Prefer the built-in ReturnType rather than reimplementing it poorly.

cards.front: How do you sketch Parameters with infer?
cards.meaning: F extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never binds P to the argument tuple. Function I/O types should use ReturnType and Parameters rather than custom copies.
cards.example: type MyParameters<F> = F extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never;

cards.front: How do you sketch recursive Awaited with infer?
cards.meaning: T extends Promise<infer U> ? MyAwaited<U> : T unwraps nested promises until a non-Promise remains. MyAwaited<Promise<Promise<string>>> is string. Prefer the built-in Awaited to unwrap Promise.

cards.front: Interview one-liner: what is infer, and how does ReturnType use it?
cards.meaning: infer captures a matched piece of a type in a conditional and reuses it in the result. ReturnType is roughly F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never. Practically: type UserDto = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof userService.findById>> so DTOs do not drift from the service.

cards.front: Can a conditional use more than one infer?
cards.meaning: Yes. FirstArg binds the first parameter: F extends (first: infer A, ...rest: any[]) => any ? A : never. If the pattern does not match, the false branch runs — never in many helpers.
cards.example: type FirstArg<F> = F extends (first: infer A, ...rest: any[]) => any ? A : never;

cards.front: What happens when an infer pattern does not match?
cards.meaning: The false branch runs. Helpers often use never there, so a non-matching input becomes never rather than a captured piece.

cards.front: Which built-ins should you use to filter a union or unwrap a Promise?
cards.meaning: Filter a union with Exclude or Extract — do not reinvent. Unwrap Promise with Awaited. Function I/O types with ReturnType and Parameters.

cards.front: How do you take a property type only if it is present?
cards.meaning: T extends { x: infer X } ? X : never. Same idea as IdOf: match a shape, infer the field, otherwise never.

cards.front: What is Awaited<ReturnType<typeof findById>> for?
cards.meaning: Derives the resolved DTO type from the service method so compile-time types track implementation instead of a hand-duplicated interface. A Nest/React sketch with a generic ServiceResult is usually just Awaited<ReturnType<typeof service.method>>.

cards.front: When should you write a custom conditional type?
cards.meaning: Day-to-day app code rarely needs hand-rolled conditionals; most value is using built-ins. Write a custom one when deriving from an existing function or API shape would otherwise drift, or when building a shared library util type — not for one-off DTOs. Deep recursive conditionals for one-off app DTOs are overkill and can slow the checker.

cards.front: Should you reimplement ReturnType in app code?
cards.meaning: No. Prefer built-ins first; custom conditionals when derivation removes real duplication. Reimplementing ReturnType poorly instead of using the built-in is a listed mistake. Explaining how Exclude and ReturnType work still proves interview depth beyond memorizing names.

cards.front: What happens with never extends X ? A : B?
cards.meaning: never distributes, which can surprise you because never is an empty union — distribution over no members yields never. Empty-union distribution is the edge case to name.
cards.notes: never extends X is not a simple 'never is assignable to everything' interview shortcut once distribution applies.

cards.front: Does the order of extends checks matter?
cards.meaning: Yes, for overlapping patterns. Put more specific patterns first, like overload order. A later, broader match can steal cases the specific branch should have taken.

cards.front: Why avoid any in conditional checks?
cards.meaning: any extends X can behave oddly and take both branches in edge cases. Avoid baking any into conditional logic.

cards.front: Is type-level extends the same as class inheritance?
cards.meaning: No. Read extends as assignability. Reading it as inheritance-only is a listed misconception and will mis-explain conditionals.

cards.front: Why do people expect ToArray<string | number> to be (string | number)[]?
cards.meaning: They forget distribution. A naked T distributes, so you get string[] | number[] unless you wrap T to disable it. That expectation without disabling distribution is a listed trap.

cards.front: How do conditionals connect to Exclude and Extract?
cards.meaning: T extends U ? is a type-level if. Naked T distributes over unions, and that distribution is how Exclude and Extract filter members.

cards.front: How does infer connect to ReturnType, Parameters, and ElementType?
cards.meaning: infer R binds a matched piece; ReturnType, Parameters, and ElementType are that pattern on function returns, argument tuples, and array elements.

cards.front: How does Promise<infer U> connect to Awaited?
cards.meaning: Matching Promise and inferring U, then recursing, is the Awaited unwrap. Nested Promise<Promise<string>> becomes string.

cards.front: How do conditionals relate to mapped types?
cards.meaning: Mapped types transform keys and properties; they are often combined with conditionals to filter keys or branch value types. Utility types consume both.

cards.front: What must you be able to say first about T extends U ? X : Y?
cards.meaning: Read it as assignability branching, not inheritance. Then explain distribution with string[] | number[] vs (string | number)[], define infer, sketch ReturnType and recursive Awaited, and say when to stop at built-ins.
